name: Carl DeMaio
title: California State Assemblymember
district: California State Assembly District 75 (San Diego County)
years_of_service: December 2, 2024 to present in the Assembly, his current elected office. DeMaio previously served on the San Diego City Council (District 5), 2008 to 2012, and was not otherwise a state legislator before his 2024 Assembly election. (Source: official California State Assembly member page, assembly.ca.gov/assemblymembers/75; Wikipedia, Carl DeMaio.)
background: DeMaio was born September 14, 1974, in Dubuque, Iowa, to teachers Carl Joseph and Diane M. DeMaio; his family relocated to Orange County, California in the late 1970s. He attended St. Catherine's Military Academy through eighth grade before winning a scholarship to Georgetown Preparatory School in Maryland in 1989. His mother died of breast cancer in 1990, and his father left the family shortly before her death. He graduated from Georgetown Prep in 1993 and earned a degree in international politics and business from Georgetown University's School of Foreign Service in 1996. (Source: Wikipedia, Carl DeMaio.)

After college, DeMaio founded The Performance Institute, a firm training government officials on performance measurement and budgeting, and in 2003 founded the American Strategic Management Institute for corporate financial training; he sold both companies to Thompson Publishing Group in late 2007. Between 1994 and 1999 he worked for the Congressional Institute on congressional budget-process training, and from 2000 worked at the Reason Foundation on government management-improvement plans. He moved to San Diego in 2002 and in 2004 launched the San Diego Citizens Budget Project, which challenged the city's budget projections and built his public profile as a fiscal-reform advocate before he ran for office. (Source: Wikipedia, Carl DeMaio.)

DeMaio was elected to the San Diego City Council (District 5) in 2008, winning his primary with 66% of the vote; he was the first openly gay man elected to the council and the first Italian American elected to San Diego city office since the 1930s. As the council's primary author of San Diego Proposition B, a June 2012 city-charter amendment replacing defined-benefit pensions with 401(k)-style plans for most new city employees, capping pensionable pay, and requiring voter approval for future pension-benefit increases, he led the campaign that passed the measure by roughly a 2-to-1 margin on June 5, 2012. (Source: Wikipedia, Carl DeMaio; this profile could not reach Ballotpedia's dedicated page for the measure, which returned an HTTP 403 error on every direct and r.jina.ai-proxied fetch attempt, so Wikipedia is used explicitly as the source for this measure's details.)

DeMaio left the council in 2012 to run for Mayor of San Diego, placing first in the primary with 31.42% before losing the general election to Democrat Bob Filner, 47.5% to 52.5%; then-Mayor Jerry Sanders endorsed DeMaio ahead of the general. He ran for the U.S. House in California's 52nd District in 2014, finishing second to Scott Peters in the primary (36% to 42%) and losing the general election 48.41% to 51.59%; media coverage noted he was among the first congressional candidates to feature a same-sex partner in a campaign ad. He ran again for the U.S. House in California's 50th District in 2020, finishing third in the primary with 19.9% and then backing Republican Darrell Issa, who won the seat. (Source: Wikipedia, Carl DeMaio.)

Between campaigns, DeMaio built Reform California, a political advocacy organization he chairs; its own site states it originated in 2003 around opposition to state budget policy under Gov. Gray Davis, while Wikipedia dates the formal organization to 2015, a discrepancy this profile notes rather than resolves. Reform California describes itself as a statewide grassroots movement with over 50,000 donors and says it has helped defeat more than 300 local and state tax measures. DeMaio led the organization's successful 2017 recall of Democratic state senator Josh Newman over his vote for a gas-tax increase, the first successful recall of a California state senator in over a century, and its 2018 campaign for a statewide gas-tax repeal initiative (Proposition 6), which voters rejected 55% to 45%. Because DeMaio chairs this organization, its own published material about his career is cited here as content from an advocacy group he leads, not as neutral reporting. (Source: reformcalifornia.org, About page, fetched via r.jina.ai; Wikipedia, Carl DeMaio.)

DeMaio was elected to the California State Assembly in 2024, succeeding the term-limited Marie Waldron in District 75. He won the primary with 42.9% against fellow Republican Andrew Hayes (18.7%, in a field that also included three Democratic candidates), then won the general election, a same-party top-two race against Hayes, 57.02% to 43% of roughly 212,500 ballots cast. He was sworn in December 2, 2024. (Source: Wikipedia, Carl DeMaio.)

In this term, DeMaio is a co-proponent of 2026 Proposition 39, the voter identification and citizenship-verification constitutional amendment, filed with the Attorney General on July 16, 2025 alongside State Sen. Tony Strickland and Donald DiCostanzo, and he chairs Reform California, which per that measure's own funding disclosures is one of the two major Yes on 39 support committees. Full detail on the measure itself, its funding, and the campaign is covered in content/measures/ca-prop-39-2026.json and is not duplicated here.

voting_record_highlights: AB 1346 (2025 to 2026), amending public-postsecondary-education residency rules for dependents of Armed Forces members: DeMaio was the author. It passed the Senate floor 39 to 0 on August 27, 2026 and was enrolled and presented to Gov. Gavin Newsom on September 8, 2026; as of this profile's research date the Governor had not yet acted on it, so it is not yet confirmed signed into law. (Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill status for AB 1346, fetched via r.jina.ai.)

AB 25 (2025 to 2026), the "California Voter ID and Election Integrity Act of 2025," a statutory predecessor to the themes later carried by the Proposition 39 initiative: DeMaio was the author. It failed passage in the Assembly Elections Committee, and a motion for reconsideration also failed 2 ayes to 5 noes on April 9, 2025, after which the bill died under Joint Rule 62(a) without further action. (Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill status for AB 25, fetched via r.jina.ai.)

AB 1993 (2025 to 2026), requiring identification information on vote-by-mail return envelopes: DeMaio was the author. The Assembly Elections Committee held a hearing on March 25, 2026 at which the measure failed passage, and the bill died without further action on April 28, 2026 under Joint Rule 62(a); the specific committee vote tally was not available in the bill-status record consulted. (Source: leginfo.legislature.ca.gov bill status for AB 1993, fetched via r.jina.ai.)
attendance: No individually published floor-attendance or voting-participation record for Assemblymember DeMaio was found. The California State Assembly does not publish a per-member attendance scorecard; the only public records located are bill-by-bill committee and floor votes at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, which is what the voting-record entries above are drawn from. This profile could not reach CalMatters' Digital Democracy tool (calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org), which for other legislators tracks bill-passage counts and vote-alignment percentages, because its search page returned a server error on every attempt during this research session; it may still hold a profile for DeMaio that a future update could check.
